paragraphs: This paper studies sparse linear regression when privacy must be protected locally and each user holds multiple observations. Sparsity means that only a small subset of the available variables matters. Earlier item-level privacy results included an error rate that grew linearly with the full number of variables, making high-dimensional problems particularly difficult.

The authors investigate user-level privacy with n users contributing m samples each. Their framework first identifies candidate variables, then estimates the model within that smaller space. They establish an error upper bound of O(s/(nmε²)), removing the linear dimension factor from the earlier O(sd/(nmε²)) rate. Here, s represents sparsity, d the full dimension, and ε the privacy parameter.

The framework also extends to more general sparse estimation problems with tight error bounds. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the proposed methods. Together, the results suggest that how samples are distributed across users matters: access to multiple samples per user can improve locally private estimation even when the total sample count stays the same.
icml-2024-better-locally-private-sparse-.tldr: Using multiple samples per user enables a locally private sparse-estimation framework whose error bound removes a linear dependence on data dimension.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models across distributed clients holding sensitive data. Much of its research addresses differences among participating clients, but this paper focuses on a different challenge: performance on clients that never joined training. The authors observe substantial degradation on these unseen clients and identify a tension between generalization and the communication or computation costs of existing approaches.

Their method, Topology-aware Federated Learning, represents relationships among clients as a graph. One module learns those relationships in a privacy-preserving way. A second module uses the resulting graph to identify influential clients and incorporates that information into the training optimization. Client relationships therefore become an explicit input to how the shared model is learned.

Evaluations across several real-world datasets support improved robustness on unseen clients alongside scalability. The contribution is a way to use the structure of the participating population to help models generalize beyond it. The reported evidence connects those two objectives, rather than treating robustness and distributed training efficiency as separate problems.
icml-2024-beyond-the-federation-topology.tldr: Topology-aware Federated Learning uses learned client relationships to improve generalization to unseen clients while supporting scalable training.

paragraphs: Convolution is difficult to define uniformly on graphs because graphs have irregular structures and lack a standard coordinate system. Existing spatial and spectral definitions provide different, relatively inflexible ways to combine information. This paper proposes Continuous Kernel Graph Convolution, or CKGConv, as a more general framework for defining that operation.

CKGConv uses graph positional encodings to derive pseudo-coordinates. It then represents convolution kernels as continuous functions of those coordinates. This gives the kernel a structured way to depend on graph position despite the absence of ordinary coordinates. The authors show theoretically that the framework includes many existing graph convolutions and has substantial expressive power.

In particular, their expressiveness result places CKGConv on par with graph transformers for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, meaning graphs with genuinely different connectivity structures. Experiments across multiple graph datasets show networks built with CKGConv outperforming existing graph convolutional networks and performing comparably to leading graph transformers. These results support continuous kernels as a flexible basis for graph learning, with both theoretical and empirical evidence.
icml-2024-ckgconv-general-graph-convolut.tldr: CKGConv defines graph convolution through continuous kernels over positional pseudo-coordinates, combining broad theoretical expressiveness with competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Instance retrieval often improves an initial ranking by propagating similarity through a nearest-neighbor graph. The idea is that nearby examples can reinforce useful matches. However, connections based only on pairs of instances can also spread misleading information from outliers or from different underlying groups, reducing retrieval accuracy.

Cluster-Aware Similarity diffusion changes where this propagation occurs. It diffuses similarity within local clusters, explicitly reducing influence from other groups. The method also introduces Bidirectional Similarity Diffusion, which adds an inverse constraint to the optimization objective to obtain a symmetric, smooth similarity matrix. A further neighbor-guided smoothing step encourages agreement among each instance's local neighbors.

These components address related aspects of the same problem: controlling which examples exchange similarity information and making the resulting relationships consistent. Evaluations on instance retrieval and object re-identification support the effectiveness of the approach. The findings suggest that the structure used to propagate similarity matters alongside the initial pairwise scores, because a poorly organized graph can amplify misleading relationships.
icml-2024-cluster-aware-similarity-diffu.tldr: Cluster-Aware Similarity diffusion improves retrieval by restricting similarity propagation to local clusters and smoothing neighboring relationships.

paragraphs: Retrieving external knowledge can help language models answer factual questions, but long retrieved passages can also make hallucination worse. This paper addresses the problem of directing a model toward useful evidence within a lengthy context. Its method, COFT, highlights important text at several levels of detail.

COFT has three stages. A recaller uses a knowledge graph to identify potentially important entities in the context. A scorer assigns those entities contextual importance weights. A selector then applies a dynamic threshold and highlights the associated paragraphs, sentences, or individual words. The coarse-to-fine structure allows emphasis to range from broader passages down to specific pieces of text.

Experiments on a knowledge-hallucination benchmark report effectiveness, including an F1 improvement described as exceeding 30%. The authors also report applicability to long-form reading comprehension and question answering. The central finding is that retrieving knowledge and making relevant knowledge salient are distinct parts of the task: organizing emphasis within retrieved material can improve how a model uses that material.
icml-2024-coarse-to-fine-highlighting-re.tldr: COFT reduces factual hallucination by identifying important entities and highlighting relevant evidence from paragraphs down to individual words.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection often assumes access to a large collection of normal examples. In practice, removing every anomaly from an unlabeled dataset may require unrealistic resources. This paper instead asks how to recover the normal-data distribution when the main training dataset contains anomalous examples.

The proposed approach supplements that contaminated dataset with two small datasets containing partially observed normal and anomalous samples. An adversarial learning scheme uses this additional information to learn the normal distribution. The authors prove that recovery is possible under stated mild conditions. Because the supplementary datasets are small, they also develop a flipping mechanism with a correctness guarantee to alleviate overfitting.

The analysis additionally considers situations where the observed anomalies do not cover every anomaly type. Experiments show the method outperforming representative baselines on contaminated datasets. The contribution therefore combines a practical change in the data requirement with conditional theoretical support: a small amount of additional normal and anomalous information can help learn normal behavior without requiring the large dataset to be completely cleaned.
icml-2024-contamination-resilient-anomal.tldr: An adversarial method uses small supplementary normal and anomalous datasets to learn normal behavior from contaminated data, with conditional recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy may need to transfer between environments whose dynamics differ. This paper considers abundant source-domain data but only limited interaction with the target domain. The challenge is to use the available source experience while accounting for behaviors that do not carry over reliably.

The authors learn representations only from the target domain, then measure their deviations on source-domain transitions. They show that these deviations can indicate a mismatch in dynamics. Their analysis also connects representation deviation to an upper bound on the difference in a policy's performance between the two domains, motivating its use as a reward penalty.

The learned representations remain separate from the policy and value function; their role is solely to penalize rewards associated with mismatch. This separation makes the adaptation signal an explicit correction to how source experience is valued. Experiments involving kinematic and morphology differences show strong performance on many tasks. The results support representation deviation as a useful transfer signal when target interaction is limited.
icml-2024-cross-domain-policy-adaptation.tldr: Target-domain representation deviations provide a reward penalty that helps policies adapt from abundant source data to different target dynamics.

paragraphs: Decision-focused learning trains a model through the decisions produced by an optimization problem. Distributionally robust optimization makes decisions while considering a set of possible probability distributions, called an ambiguity set. This paper addresses how to differentiate those decisions with respect to that set, allowing robust optimization to become part of a learning pipeline.

The authors develop differentiable layers for mixed-integer problems with parameterized second-order conic ambiguity sets and discuss extensions to Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Mixed-integer decisions contain both continuous and discrete components. Their dual-view methodology treats these components using different principles, implemented through a differentiable energy-based surrogate whose gradient is estimated with importance sampling.

They prove an asymptotic convergence property for the surrogate under regularization. They also build a contextual decision-focused learning pipeline and compare it experimentally with a prediction-focused approach. The contribution supplies machinery for training through robust decisions, including discrete choices, so that learning can respond to the optimization outcome and the uncertainty description that shapes it.
icml-2024-differentiable-distributionall.tldr: Differentiable robust-optimization layers enable learning through mixed continuous and discrete decisions and the ambiguity sets that shape them.

paragraphs: One way to train a control policy is to predict future rewards with a learned world model and backpropagate through those predictions. Over long horizons, this can create an optimization problem that is difficult to navigate. This paper asks whether transformers, known for propagating gradients over long sequences, resolve that difficulty.

The authors find that commonly used transformer world models can still create indirect gradient paths that harm long-range policy learning. They propose Action-conditioned World Models, or AWMs, designed to give gradients more direct routes. Their policy-gradient framework makes explicit how the world model's architecture determines the updates used to train the policy.

The authors demonstrate that AWMs can create easier optimization landscapes even compared with those obtained from the simulator itself. Transformer AWMs also produce better policies than competitive baselines on realistic long-horizon tasks. The findings show why choosing a transformer architecture alone is insufficient: the path connecting actions to future outcomes also affects the usefulness of the learning signal.
icml-2024-do-transformer-world-models-gi.tldr: Action-conditioned World Models improve long-horizon policy learning by giving gradients more direct paths than commonly used transformer world models.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information using neuron-like spikes, offering an alternative way to model temporal data. Applying them to forecasting is challenging because the data must be encoded and aligned with the network's temporal processing. The authors also identify a lack of standardized guidance for choosing suitable models.

This paper proposes a framework for using spiking neural networks in time-series forecasting. Its central motivation is to take advantage of spiking neurons' efficiency when processing information over time. Alongside forecasting experiments, the authors conduct targeted analyses of whether the networks capture dependencies within time series, examining their ability to represent temporal dynamics.

Across diverse benchmarks, the proposed approaches achieve comparable or better forecasting results than traditional methods while consuming much less energy. The analysis experiments provide further insight into the networks' temporal modeling strengths. These findings support spiking networks as a promising forecasting alternative, with the appeal coming from the combination of predictive performance and energy efficiency demonstrated in the reported evaluations.
icml-2024-efficient-and-effective-time-s.tldr: A spiking-network forecasting framework achieves competitive accuracy across diverse benchmarks with substantially lower reported energy consumption.

paragraphs: Neuro-symbolic reinforcement learning combines learned perception with symbolic policies that can be inspected. For visual tasks, it needs structured descriptions of the observed state. Earlier methods struggled to refine those descriptions using rewards efficiently, and understanding the resulting symbolic policies still required substantial domain knowledge.

The proposed framework jointly learns structured states and symbolic policies. It first distills a vision foundation model into an efficient perception module, then refines that module during policy learning. This connects the visual representation to the reward-driven learning process, allowing perception and decision-making to develop together instead of leaving the structured state representation fixed.

The authors also build a pipeline that prompts GPT-4 to explain learned policies and individual decisions in text. They report that these explanations substantially reduce the cognitive burden of understanding symbolic policies. Evaluation on nine Atari tasks supports the framework's effectiveness and includes generated explanations. The work addresses both how interpretable policies are learned and how their contents become accessible to users.
icml-2024-end-to-end-neuro-symbolic-rein.tldr: The framework jointly refines visual perception and symbolic policies, then uses GPT-4 to explain their decisions in text.

paragraphs: Increasing the resolution of scientific data must account for continuity, physical behavior at multiple scales, and high-frequency signals. This paper proposes an arbitrary-scale super-resolution method based on operator learning. Its resolution-invariant design learns mappings between function spaces, allowing the model to address changes in resolution within that formulation.

The model uses a hierarchical neural operator with Galerkin-type self-attention to learn these mappings efficiently. Sinc filters transfer information between levels of the hierarchy and ensure representation equivalence within the proposed operator. These architectural choices address how information is represented and moved across scales.

A separate learnable loss prior comes from spectral resizing of the input. It dynamically adjusts individual pixels' contributions to the loss, balancing gradients across the model, and is designed to be usable beyond this architecture. Experiments across datasets from different domains show consistent improvements over strong super-resolution baselines. The work combines a resolution-invariant architecture with an adaptable training objective to improve reconstruction of scientific data.
icml-2024-hierarchical-neural-operator-t.tldr: A hierarchical neural operator and learnable frequency-aware loss improve arbitrary-scale super-resolution across scientific datasets.

paragraphs: Cross-modality transfer applies a pretrained model to tasks involving a different kind of data from its original training data. Although fine-tuning can work in these settings, the authors ask how the gap between modalities affects reuse of the model's existing knowledge. Their experiments connect larger modality gaps with weaker knowledge reuse and less effective transfer.

The paper formalizes this gap through differences in the conditional distribution P(Y|X), which describes the relationship between inputs and targets. This frames the issue as knowledge misalignment between modalities. The proposed Modality Knowledge Alignment method, MoNA, uses meta-learning to learn a transformation of target data before transfer takes place.

That transformation aims to reduce the knowledge discrepancy so the pretrained model can make better use of what it already learned. Experiments show significant improvements over cross-modal fine-tuning approaches and better reuse of source-modality knowledge. The contribution links an empirical diagnosis of transfer difficulty to a method that prepares target data for more effective adaptation.
icml-2024-learning-modality-knowledge-al.tldr: MoNA learns target-data transformations that reduce modality knowledge mismatch and improve reuse of pretrained knowledge during transfer.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing offers a way to update a language model without expensive retraining. This paper examines what happens to nearby knowledge when an edit adds new information. Its specific setting is a factual question with several correct answers: adding another answer should preserve the existing correct answers and avoid introducing incorrect ones.

The authors introduce an additivity metric and construct PEAK, a benchmark for measuring these neighboring effects. The evaluation checks both the loss of previously correct answers and the accidental inclusion of wrong answers. This expands the assessment of an edit beyond whether the model can produce the newly supplied fact.

They also propose Appending via Preservation and Prevention, or APP, a plug-and-play framework designed to maintain the integrity of the answer list. Experiments combining APP with four editing methods across three language models demonstrate its effectiveness. The work makes preservation an explicit part of knowledge addition: a successful update must be assessed in relation to the surrounding answers it can disturb.
icml-2024-neighboring-perturbations-of-k.tldr: PEAK measures how knowledge additions disturb related answers, while APP helps preserve correct answers and prevent incorrect additions.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning reuses previously collected experience stored in a replay buffer. This paper asks whether online learners leave useful information in that buffer underexploited. The authors observe that an offline policy trained concurrently on the same stored data can sometimes outperform the online policy, although that advantage does not arise reliably.

Offline-Boosted Actor-Critic, or OBAC, turns this occasional advantage into an adaptive learning mechanism. It compares policy values to identify when the offline policy is better, then uses that policy as a constraint on online policy learning. The framework remains model-free and online, while drawing additional guidance from an offline learner sharing its experience.

Across 53 tasks in six suites, the authors report that OBAC outperforms popular model-free baselines and rivals advanced model-based methods in sample efficiency and final performance. The findings support using value comparisons to decide when historical behavior should guide the current learner. The key is selective assistance, since the motivating observation is that offline learning is only sometimes stronger.
icml-2024-offline-boosted-actor-critic-a.tldr: OBAC improves online reinforcement learning by adaptively using a concurrently trained offline policy when value comparisons indicate it is stronger.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning data may come from different policies or from environments whose dynamics have changed. Both situations alter the distribution of observed transitions. This paper argues that these discrepancies deserve a unified treatment because ignoring them, or relying on specialized task assumptions, can lead to weaker performance and high learning variance.

Occupancy-Matching Policy Optimization, or OMPO, builds its learning objective around differences in transition occupancy: how transitions are distributed under the relevant policies and dynamics. The authors reformulate that objective into a tractable min-max problem using duality. The implementation combines an actor-critic architecture with a distribution discriminator and a small local buffer.

Experiments cover policy shifts with stationary and changing dynamics, as well as domain adaptation, in OpenAI Gym, Meta-World, and Panda Robots environments. OMPO outperforms the specialized baselines in all evaluated settings. It performs particularly strongly when combined with domain randomization, supporting its potential for robotics. The results connect several forms of distribution shift through one policy-learning framework.
icml-2024-ompo-a-unified-framework-for-r.tldr: OMPO uses transition occupancy matching to learn policies across shifts in behavior and environment dynamics within one framework.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization compresses a trained network by reducing numerical precision, but outliers can severely damage transformer accuracy. This paper studies reconstruction granularity: the level at which the quantized model is reconstructed. The authors identify this choice as an overlooked factor in controlling the effect of outliers.

Theoretical analysis and empirical results show that granularity substantially influences quantization performance. The best choice also depends on architecture. In particular, the multi-stage Swin Transformer benefits from finer granularity, differing from the trends seen in ViT and DeiT. The authors develop an algorithm to determine an appropriate granularity for different vision transformer models.

The method achieves reported state-of-the-art post-training quantization results. At four bits, Swin-Base reaches 82.24% ImageNet top-1 accuracy versus 78.32% for RepQ-ViT, a 3.92 percentage-point gain. ViT-Small reaches 80.50% versus NoisyQuant's 76.86%. These examples support tailoring reconstruction granularity to the architecture when managing quantization errors caused by outliers, rather than assuming the same granularity works equally well across designs.
icml-2024-outlier-aware-slicing-for-post.tldr: Choosing reconstruction granularity for each transformer architecture reduces outlier-related quantization damage and improves low-precision accuracy.

paragraphs: Orthogonal fine-tuning adapts pretrained models while preserving angular relationships in parameter space, aiming to retain pretrained knowledge. This paper identifies two drawbacks: quadratic parameter complexity in dimension d and limited flexibility for adapting to downstream tasks. The proposed quasi-Givens Orthogonal Fine-Tuning method, qGOFT, addresses both issues.

The authors first use a construction based on Givens rotations and establish a provable equivalence for the orthogonal transformation they describe. They report reducing parameter complexity from O(d²) to O(d). This makes the transformation substantially more parameter-efficient within their formulation, addressing the cost of adapting very large pretrained models.

The method then softens strict orthogonality through regularization, permitting adjustments to norms and relative angles. These extra degrees of freedom are intended to accommodate semantic differences in downstream tasks while retaining an orthogonality-based constraint. Experiments across multiple tasks and pretrained models validate the methods' effectiveness. The overall contribution combines a compact rotation-based parameterization with controlled flexibility for adaptation.
icml-2024-parameter-efficient-quasi-orth.tldr: qGOFT combines a parameter-efficient Givens-rotation construction with soft orthogonality constraints to make pretrained-model adaptation more flexible.

paragraphs: Predicting a multi-agent system requires modeling how agents influence one another over time. Graph neural networks can represent those interactions, but changes in the system and complicated interaction rules remain challenging. PGODE addresses this by combining contextual information with a continuous-time graph model of the dynamics.

The method extracts two kinds of context from historical trajectories using representation disentanglement and system parameters: information about individual objects and information about the system as a whole. Separating them allows their influences to be modeled independently. These representations then determine a combination of interaction prototypes within a graph ordinary differential equation model, increasing its ability to express different behaviors.

PGODE is trained end to end through variational inference to maximize likelihood. Experiments both within and outside the training distribution show it outperforming the compared baselines. The stated results support the idea that explicitly separating object-level and system-level influences can help a dynamics model generalize when the system changes, while prototype combinations provide flexibility for modeling interactions.
icml-2024-pgode-towards-high-quality-sys.tldr: PGODE combines disentangled object and system context with interaction prototypes to improve continuous-time modeling of multi-agent dynamics.

paragraphs: This position paper questions how offline reinforcement learning is currently assessed for dynamic treatment regimes, where treatment decisions unfold over time. The authors identify inconsistent evaluation metrics, missing naive and supervised-learning baselines, and variation in how researchers formulate the decision problem. These choices can complicate claims about an algorithm's quality.

A case study on a public sepsis dataset includes more than 17,000 evaluation experiments. It shows that reported reinforcement learning performance can change substantially with the evaluation metric and Markov decision process formulation. In some cases, random baselines receive better evaluations than reinforcement learning algorithms under the chosen policy-evaluation methods and reward design.

These findings concern the reliability of the evaluation setup; they do not establish that random treatment decisions produce better patient outcomes. The authors call for more careful policy evaluation and algorithm development and discuss possible improvements. Their central argument is that progress in this application requires examining how conclusions depend on the definitions, comparisons, and evaluation procedures used to produce them.
icml-2024-position-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: A large sepsis evaluation study shows that conclusions about treatment-policy reinforcement learning can depend strongly on metrics and problem formulation.

paragraphs: Potential-based motion planning represents motion constraints through functions that can be added together. This makes it convenient to combine different requirements for a robot's movement. The difficulty is finding a good path through the resulting potential landscape, especially in high-dimensional spaces where optimization can become trapped in local minima.

The proposed approach learns potentials over complete motion-planning trajectories with a neural network. The goal is to obtain potentials that are easier to optimize, addressing the difficulty of constructing paths from a challenging configuration-space landscape. It retains the compositional structure that makes potential-based planning attractive while learning the functions used to guide planning.

The authors demonstrate substantial improvements over both classical and recent learned planning approaches, along with avoidance of local-minimum problems in their evaluations. They also demonstrate generalization to many different motion constraints through composition. The stated findings support learning an optimization-friendly trajectory potential as a way to combine flexible constraints with more effective path construction.
icml-2024-potential-based-diffusion-moti.tldr: Learning easily optimized potentials over motion trajectories improves planning while preserving the ability to combine different motion constraints.

paragraphs: Decision Transformer uses sequence modeling for reinforcement learning, but this paper identifies a weakness in combining useful portions of imperfect recorded trajectories. Recalling trajectories from a dataset does not necessarily provide the ability to stitch those portions into better behavior. The authors examine this issue through hierarchical reinforcement learning.

Their general framework separates each decision into two stages. A high-level policy proposes a prompt suited to the current state, and a low-level policy chooses an action conditioned on that prompt. They show that Decision Transformer is a special case under particular choices of these policies and discuss how those choices can fail.

The authors then study joint optimization of the two policies to enable trajectory stitching, leading to new offline reinforcement learning algorithms. Experiments show significant improvements over Decision Transformer on several control and navigation benchmarks. The contribution is both an explanation of an existing limitation and a design route: learning what to ask the action policy to do can improve how stored experience is combined.
icml-2024-rethinking-decision-transforme.tldr: A hierarchical view of Decision Transformer leads to jointly trained prompt and action policies that better combine useful parts of offline trajectories.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation requires understanding the environment and selecting actions that serve a goal. This paper argues that existing uses of large multimodal models can generalize poorly to unfamiliar tasks or scenes and can overlook relevant multimodal information. RoboMP² addresses these issues by organizing the system around distinct perception and planning components.

The Goal-Conditioned Multimodal Perceptor uses a tailored multimodal language model to capture environment states through semantic reasoning and localization. The Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Planner then retrieves relevant policies through a coarse-to-fine search. It supplies the k most relevant policies as in-context demonstrations to help the planner produce an appropriate plan.

The framework therefore connects goal-aware scene understanding with selected examples of behavior. Experiments on the VIMA benchmark and real-world tasks report superiority over the compared baselines, with improvement of around 10%. The findings support combining specialized multimodal perception with retrieval-guided planning for manipulation, rather than depending solely on a large model's general reasoning ability.
icml-2024-robomp-2-a-robotic-multimodal-.tldr: RoboMP² combines goal-conditioned multimodal perception with retrieval of relevant policy demonstrations to improve robotic manipulation planning.

paragraphs: Consistency Models aim to generate samples in a single step. This paper provides a convergence guarantee explaining when their output distribution can be close to the real data distribution. The main result bounds Wasserstein-2 error under assumptions about score-matching error, consistency error, and the smoothness of the data distribution.

The analysis requires L² accuracy, an average-error condition, for the score and consistency functions rather than uniform L∞ accuracy. It avoids strong distributional assumptions such as log-Sobolev conditions and has polynomial dependence on all parameters. The authors state that the resulting guarantee matches leading convergence guarantees for score-based generative models.

They also show that multistep consistency sampling can reduce error further. Extensions cover arbitrary bounded distributions, including those supported on lower-dimensional submanifolds. With Langevin-based modifications to the output, the analysis additionally yields total-variation error guarantees. These results give conditional mathematical support for efficient sampling and distinguish the guarantees available for one-step, multistep, and modified output procedures.
icml-2024-sampling-is-as-easy-as-keeping.tldr: The paper establishes conditional convergence guarantees for Consistency Models and shows how additional sampling steps or output modifications strengthen error guarantees.

paragraphs: Two-component mixed linear regression learns two regression models from observations whose component labels are unknown. Expectation-Maximization is widely used for this problem. Earlier work established fast convergence in certain settings, but left the precise super-linear convergence exponent and the geometry of the sequence of estimates insufficiently understood.

The authors derive explicit EM update expressions using Bessel functions across all signal-to-noise regimes. They then focus on the noiseless setting, deriving a population-level recurrence that completely characterizes the iterations. A striking result is that the iterates lie on a particular cycloid, giving the algorithm's progress a concrete geometric description.

This trajectory-based analysis yields a theoretical estimate of the super-linear convergence exponent and improves the statistical error bound for finite samples. The distinctions between settings matter: the closed-form updates cover all noise regimes, while the cycloid characterization concerns noiseless population dynamics. The paper's contribution is a geometric framework that connects the path taken by EM to its convergence speed and estimation error.
icml-2024-unveiling-the-cycloid-trajecto.tldr: A cycloid characterization of noiseless population EM reveals its convergence behavior and supports sharper analysis of two-component mixed linear regression.
